questions.q: What distinguishes a real architecture review, as modeled in this lesson, from a 'looks good, ship it' rubber stamp?
options: A real review focuses only on whether the quantum result beat a classical baseline
A real review is always shorter than a rubber-stamp approval
A real review never identifies any remaining open items

A real review names what was checked against a specific standard (e.g., the five Lesson 5 mistakes) with concrete evidence from the run log, and explicitly surfaces open items rather than letting them disappear
questions.explain: The lesson's sign-off example cites specific checklist items with log evidence and explicitly names the unresolved $21,120/month projection as an open item -- exactly the specificity and honesty that distinguishes it from a vague approval.

questions.q: How did this capstone project specifically address Lesson 5's Mistake 3 (no cost ceiling on the optimization loop)?
options: Lesson 21's circuit-breaker checks cumulative ledger cost after every submission and halts the loop if it crosses $1,200 (25% headroom over the $960 plan), independent of the iteration counter
By assuming the loop would always converge before becoming expensive, with no explicit check
By refusing to track cost at all, since cost tracking wasn't part of this project
By relying solely on a maximum iteration count with no dollar-based check
questions.explain: The project's specific fix was a circuit-breaker checked after every submission against a $1,200 ceiling with headroom -- an explicit, dollar-based safeguard independent of the iteration count, directly addressing Mistake 3.

questions.q: The lesson flags that the $21,120/month daily-run cost projection from Lesson 19's kickoff 'was never resolved -- just flagged.' Why does the lesson treat this as a problem for the final review to address?
options: This issue should be ignored since the capstone only needed to run once
The $21,120/month figure was actually incorrect and should be deleted from the record
A genuine second-pass review has to revisit flagged-but-unresolved scoping concerns rather than letting them quietly disappear once a single successful run makes the project feel 'done'
Monthly cost projections are irrelevant once a single run succeeds
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues that getting one run to work shouldn't let an earlier flagged business-cost concern quietly vanish -- a genuine review re-surfaces it and recommends a follow-up conversation before any production rollout.

questions.q: According to the lesson, which parts of this capstone's architecture carry over unchanged if the ansatz and cost function are swapped for a QAOA combinatorial problem or a variational classifier?
options: Only the quantum circuit code carries over; all classical orchestration must be rebuilt
The state machine, batching strategy, retry/fallback decision table, cost ledger/circuit-breaker, and simulator-first testing discipline -- the entire classical orchestration pattern
Only the cost ledger carries over; everything else is VQE-specific
Nothing carries over; a completely new architecture would be required for any different algorithm
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that the classical orchestration pattern -- state machine, batching, retry/fallback logic, cost tracking, and simulator-first testing -- is algorithm-agnostic and transfers to any Pattern A hybrid workload, which is the actual reusable deliverable of the course.

questions.q: What should be true of every number in the completed run's operational story (e.g., total cost, wall-clock time, retry count), according to the lesson?
options: Numbers in the operational story are expected to be unverifiable estimates
The numbers only need to be approximately correct, with no requirement for traceability
Only the final cost figure needs to be accurate; intermediate numbers don't matter
Each number should be traceable to a specific ledger entry or log line -- if a number can only be explained by 'that sounds about right,' the logging isn't complete enough yet
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly requires that every reported number be traceable to specific logged evidence -- an untraceable number is a sign that the cost/latency logging built in Lesson 21 isn't actually complete.
